risk_rationale: The 10Y yield has surged 57bp to 4.99%, compressing the 10Y-2Y spread to just 29bp and tightening financial conditions materially across mortgages, credit, and equity discount rates. NFP collapsed to 29K — an 86K sequential drop — signaling rapid labor market deterioration even as core PCE holds at 3.0%, leaving the Fed with no clean exit. WTI at $103.4 and Brent at $123.1 sustain an energy-driven inflation floor that complicates any pivot narrative.
outlook_headline: Stagflation risk is no longer theoretical: labor is cracking while inflation remains above target and rates are still rising.
outlook_body: The macro regime has shifted decisively toward late-cycle stress, with the labor market sending a clear deceleration signal — 29K NFP is recessionary territory by any historical benchmark. The Fed faces a genuine policy trap: core PCE at 3.0% and headline CPI at 3.7% preclude easing, yet the rate structure at current levels is actively destroying demand in housing, autos, and leveraged credit. Energy prices are the wildcard — the $19.7 Brent-WTI spread reflects supply fragmentation and geopolitical risk premium that could push headline inflation higher regardless of domestic demand weakness. Portfolios should be positioned defensively with duration risk actively managed and credit exposure concentrated in high-quality IG.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP growth at 2.2% annualized is still positive but is almost certainly a backward-looking read that predates the full impact of the 10Y spike, the NFP collapse, and sustained energy prices. The consumption engine — which drives roughly 70% of GDP — faces simultaneous headwinds from a 7.32% mortgage rate, a 4.1% savings rate with limited buffer, and decelerating payroll growth. A sub-1% or negative GDP print in the next one to two quarters is a credible base case if current financial conditions persist.
tabs.jobs: NFP at 29K is an 86K sequential decline and represents a critical deterioration signal — this is not noise, it is a trend break. Wage growth at 3.9% YoY remains above the Fed's comfort zone, but decelerating payrolls will compress aggregate income growth and consumer spending capacity within one to two quarters. The combination of collapsing job creation and still-elevated wages is consistent with a labor market that is tightening from the demand side, not the supply side — a recessionary configuration.
tabs.unemp: U-3 unemployment at 4.2% has not yet moved to alarm levels, but U-6 at 7.6% reveals meaningful underemployment and labor market slack beneath the headline. The 340bp gap between U-6 and U-3 indicates a significant share of the workforce is in part-time or marginally attached positions, which will compress consumer spending durability. With NFP at 29K, U-3 is a lagging indicator that will likely move higher over the next two to three months.
tabs.wages: Wages at 3.9% YoY remain above the Fed's implicit ~3.0-3.5% comfort zone for a 2% inflation target, but the real wage gain against CPI of 3.7% is essentially zero (+0.2pp). Workers are not accumulating real purchasing power, which constrains consumption durability even as nominal wages look resilient. The wage-price spiral risk is diminishing, but wages are not decelerating fast enough to give the Fed confidence to ease.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.7% YoY is running 170bp above the Fed's 2% target, driven in part by energy — WTI at $103.4 ensures no near-term relief on that component. Core CPI at 2.6% is more contained but still above target, and the gap between headline and core reflects energy pass-through risk that could re-accelerate if Brent sustains above $120. The Fed cannot declare victory on inflation with this data configuration, regardless of labor market softening.
tabs.pce: Core PCE at 3.0% is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge and it remains 100bp above target — this is the binding constraint on any dovish pivot. The savings rate at 4.1% is low by historical standards, suggesting consumers have limited buffer to absorb further income shocks from job losses or energy costs. Headline PCE at 3.4% confirms that inflation is broad-based and not solely an energy artifact, reinforcing the Fed's on-hold posture.
tabs.yield: The 10Y yield at 4.99% — up 57bp from the prior snapshot — is the dominant financial conditions shock, with the 30Y mortgage now at 7.32% transmitting that pressure directly into the real economy. The 10Y-2Y spread of 29bp remains positive but is dangerously thin; any further front-end repricing on sticky inflation data could re-invert the curve. The Fed Funds rate at 3.88% implies the market is pricing additional hikes or a prolonged hold, and with core PCE at 3.0%, there is no credible basis for near-term cuts.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 88bp and HY OAS at 318bp reflect a market that has not yet fully priced the labor deterioration or the rate shock embedded in the 10Y move. HY at 318bp is not distressed, but with NFP at 29K and the 10Y at 4.99%, spread widening pressure is building — particularly in rate-sensitive and consumer-facing sectors. Credit conditions are tightening at the margin; any further deterioration in employment or earnings will accelerate spread widening and reduce primary market access for lower-rated issuers.
tabs.housing: The 30Y mortgage rate at 7.32% — up 95bp from the prior snapshot — is a severe affordability shock that is effectively locking existing homeowners in place and pricing first-time buyers out of the market. Housing Starts at 1,221K show the market has not collapsed, but at 7.32% financing costs, demand destruction is accelerating and builder cancellations will rise. The Case-Shiller HPI YoY uptick of 1.43bp to 2.09% is a lagging signal; forward-looking affordability metrics at current mortgage rates point to price pressure resuming its downward trajectory.
tabs.oil: WTI fell $6.39 to $103.37 but remains at a level that sustains significant energy inflation pass-through into headline CPI and PCE. The Brent-WTI spread of $19.73 is abnormally wide, pointing to acute international supply constraints or logistics disruptions that are not yet resolved. At $103+ WTI, energy acts as a regressive tax on consumer spending power, compounding the affordability squeeze already visible in the 4.1% savings rate.
tabs.banks: Net interest income faces a complex outlook: the 10Y at 4.99% supports asset yields, but a 29K NFP print and rising U-6 at 7.6% will pressure loan demand and increase provisioning requirements. Credit card delinquencies at 2.9% are not yet systemic but are trending in the wrong direction given the consumer income squeeze underway. Banks with heavy consumer lending exposure and variable-rate mortgage books face the sharpest earnings risk as the labor market deterioration feeds into charge-off rates over the next two quarters.

signal_flags.note: A 57bp spike in the 10Y is a major financial conditions tightening event — it reprices mortgages, corporate debt, and equity discount rates simultaneously and is the primary systemic risk in this snapshot.

An 86K sequential drop to 29K is a recessionary-level payroll print. This is not a one-month anomaly to dismiss — it signals the labor market is deteriorating rapidly and will feed into consumer spending and credit quality within quarters.

Despite the $6.39 pullback, WTI above $100 sustains energy inflation that prevents headline CPI from converging toward core. The Brent-WTI spread of $19.73 signals international supply stress that could reverse the WTI decline quickly.

A 95bp jump in the 30Y mortgage rate is a severe affordability shock — at 7.32%, monthly payments on a median-priced home are at multi-decade highs relative to income, threatening both housing demand and household balance sheets.

The uptick in home price appreciation is a lagging signal and likely reflects prior months' data before the mortgage rate spike fully transmitted. Forward affordability at 7.32% mortgage rates makes sustained HPI appreciation implausible.
